title: The All-Nighter
briefing: Chloe, 16, has a history test on Friday. On Wednesday she studies for an hour and sleeps nine hours. On Thursday she studies five more hours, until 3 a.m., and sleeps three. In the test she yawns, rereads questions, and can't recall the dates she crammed on Thursday — but Wednesday's material comes back easily.
question: Why did five extra hours of studying barely help?

clues.title: Three hours of sleep
clues.text: Up studying until 3 a.m., alarm at 6. Her usual school night is about nine hours.
clues.shows: a night far shorter than her brain needs

clues.title: Yawning, rereading questions
clues.text: She reads some questions three times before they make sense, and keeps losing her place.
clues.shows: a tired brain struggling to focus

clues.title: Wednesday's facts stuck
clues.text: What she studied on Wednesday — then slept nine hours — came back quickly and clearly.
clues.shows: material followed by a full night's sleep was stored well

clues.title: Thursday's facts gone
clues.text: The dates she crammed after midnight felt familiar but wouldn't come back, even when she wasn't rushed.
clues.shows: studying without sleep afterwards didn't get properly saved

hypotheses.text: The test was harder than the practice questions.
hypotheses.flaw: A harder test wouldn't make Wednesday's facts come back easily and Thursday's not at all.

hypotheses.text: She was too tired to concentrate during the test.
hypotheses.flaw: If it were only tiredness in the test, Wednesday's facts would be just as hard to recall as Thursday's — but they came back easily.

hypotheses.text: The extra studying didn't get stored, because memories are saved during sleep.
hypotheses.flaw: Storage alone doesn't explain the yawning and having to reread questions.

hypotheses.text: Both: sleep is when the brain stores what you studied, so Thursday night's cramming was never properly saved — and the short night also left her too tired to focus during the test.

prediction.prompt: Chloe studies the same amount each time. As she gets more hours of sleep afterwards — from 2 to 10 — what happens to how much of what she studied her brain stores?

second.question: If she studies more hours but still sleeps only three, what happens to her alertness in the test?

concepts.label: too little sleep
concepts.hint: What was different about Thursday night?

concepts.label: sleep stores memories
concepts.hint: What does the brain do with the day's learning while you sleep?

concepts.label: a tired brain
concepts.hint: How did she feel in the test?

concepts.label: hard to focus
concepts.hint: What did tiredness do during the test?

concepts.label: two separate costs
concepts.hint: Did the short night cost her one thing or two?

transfer.context: Ana and her friend practise a new dance routine for two hours on Monday evening. Ana sleeps well and dances it better on Tuesday than at the end of practice. Her friend stays up until 3 a.m. gaming, forgets half the steps on Tuesday and keeps yawning.
options: Ana's friend is a worse dancer.
Sleep stored Ana's practice and left her alert; her friend's short night meant the steps weren't stored and she was too tired to focus.
transfer.retryHint: Same practice, different nights — which of Chloe's clues compared what happened after a full night with what happened after a short one?
transfer.explanation: Both dancers practised the same amount. Ana's full night let her brain store the routine and left her alert. Her friend lost both: the steps weren't saved, and the tired brain struggled to focus on what was.

takeaway: Sleep does two jobs for learning: it stores what you studied during the day, and it leaves you alert enough to use it. An all-nighter loses both — the extra hours of study never get saved, and the tired brain struggles to find what was.
